answers.text:
I'll look into the current evidence on this.Web search isn't available to me right now, so here's what I can tell you from my existing knowledge — please verify against current literature, since head-to-head data in this space is limited.

## The key caveat first

**There are no head-to-head randomized trials of ruxolitinib cream versus tacrolimus or pimecrolimus**, and essentially none in a specifically defined "steroid-naive" population. All cross-drug comparisons are indirect (network meta-analyses or informal comparison of vehicle-controlled trials), which is problematic because the trials differ in disease severity, body surface area caps, endpoint timing, and vehicle response rates.

## Approximate monotherapy efficacy from pivotal trials

**Ruxolitinib 1.5% cream (TRuE-AD1/AD2, 8 weeks, mild-to-moderate AD, ages ≥12)**
- IGA treatment success (0/1 + ≥2-grade improvement): roughly 50–54% vs ~11–15% vehicle
- EASI-75: roughly 62–62% vs ~24–25% vehicle
- Itch NRS ≥4-point improvement: ~52% vs ~15%, with separation from vehicle within ~12 hours

**Tacrolimus 0.1% ointment (adults, 12 weeks)**
- Physician global "excellent/cleared" or ≥90% improvement: roughly 27–37% vs ~7% vehicle
- Generally considered comparable to mid-potency topical steroids in moderate-to-severe disease

**Pimecrolimus 1% cream (6 weeks, mild-to-moderate)**
- IGA 0/1: roughly 35–40% vs ~18–25% vehicle
- Consistently the weakest of the three in indirect comparisons; roughly comparable to a mild (class VII) steroid

## How to interpret this

Network meta-analyses of topical AD therapies have generally ranked ruxolitinib cream at or near the top for short-term IGA success and itch, above tacrolimus 0.1%, with pimecrolimus lowest. But the absolute gaps are inflated by differing vehicle response rates and endpoint definitions — TRuE-AD's vehicle arms performed unusually poorly, which widens the apparent treatment effect.

## On "steroid-naive" specifically

Most AD trials enroll patients with prior steroid exposure and require washout rather than true naivety. Sub-analyses by prior therapy are rarely reported. The practical corollary is that in a genuinely treatment-naive patient with mild disease, expected response to any of these will likely be higher than trial averages, and a low-cost topical steroid remains the standard first step in most guidelines — with calcineurin inhibitors and ruxolitinib reserved for sensitive sites, steroid-sparing maintenance, or steroid failure/intolerance.

Also worth factoring in: ruxolitinib cream carries a boxed warning (class JAK labeling) and BSA/duration limits (≤20% BSA, short-term/non-continuous), whereas tacrolimus and pimecrolimus carry the older malignancy boxed warning that long-term registry data have largely not borne out.

If you want, I can help you frame a search strategy for the most recent network meta-analyses on this.

answers.text:
I'll look up current guidance on this.**No — occlusion is specifically advised against with Opzelura.**

The labeling is explicit: apply a thin layer twice daily to affected areas, and do not use with occlusive dressings.

**Why this matters more than with a topical steroid:**

Ruxolitinib is a JAK inhibitor that is meaningfully absorbed through skin. Pharmacokinetic studies suggest about 6% of topically applied ruxolitinib is systemically absorbed, and plasma concentrations — particularly if applied to more than 20% of BSA — may fall within the range reached with oral ruxolitinib. That's why Opzelura carries a boxed warning class-labeled from oral JAK inhibitors, covering serious infections, including TB and bacterial, fungal, and viral infections that can spread throughout the body, with some people hospitalized or dying, and serious lung infections reported with OPZELURA itself. Occluding would push absorption toward systemic exposure territory without any efficacy data to justify it.

**The guardrails that come with it:**
- Atopic dermatitis: up to 20% BSA; vitiligo: up to 10% BSA
- No more than one 60 g tube per week or one 100 g tube per 2 weeks
- Not recommended in combination with therapeutic biologics, other JAK inhibitors, or potent immunosuppressants such as azathioprine or cyclosporine

**If you're occluding because it isn't working:** that's the real issue to raise with your prescriber. For vitiligo especially, response is slow — treatment for longer than 24 weeks may be needed for a satisfactory response, and if there's no meaningful repigmentation by 24 weeks the patient should be reevaluated. For eczema, re-examination is advised if there's no improvement within 8 weeks. Adding narrowband UVB (for vitiligo) or switching agents are legitimate escalation strategies your dermatologist can discuss; occlusion isn't one of them.

One nuance: normal clothing over treated skin is fine — the prohibition is on deliberate occlusive dressings (plastic wrap, hydrocolloid, occlusive tape, "wet wrap" style therapy).

Worth a message to your prescriber before changing anything.

drafts.content_md:
## Direct answer

**OPZELURA (ruxolitinib) cream 1.5% is FDA-approved for mild to moderate atopic dermatitis in patients 2 years of age and older — not 12 years and older.** The 12-and-older age limit applies only to the separate nonsegmental vitiligo indication. The two indications are distinct and should not be combined.

## The two indications, line by line

- **Atopic dermatitis (age 2+):** OPZELURA is indicated for the topical short-term and non-continuous chronic treatment of mild to moderate atopic dermatitis in non-immunocompromised adult and pediatric patients **2 years of age and older** whose disease is not adequately controlled with topical prescription therapies or when those therapies are not advisable.
- **Nonsegmental vitiligo (age 12+):** OPZELURA is indicated for the topical treatment of nonsegmental vitiligo in adult and pediatric patients **12 years of age and older**.

**Limitations of Use:** Use of OPZELURA in combination with therapeutic biologics, other JAK inhibitors, or potent immunosuppressants such as azathioprine or cyclosporine is not recommended.

## Dosing differs by age in atopic dermatitis

Apply a thin layer twice daily to affected areas of up to 20% body surface area. Do not use with occlusive dressings.

| Age group (atopic dermatitis) | Maximum amount |
|---|---|
| Adults and pediatric patients 12 years and older | No more than one 60 g tube per week or one 100 g tube per 2 weeks |
| Pediatric patients 2 to 11 years | No more than one 60 g tube per 2 weeks |

Stop using when signs and symptoms (e.g., itch, rash, and redness) of atopic dermatitis resolve. If signs and symptoms do not improve within 8 weeks, patients should be re-examined by their healthcare provider.

## Questions and answers

**What is the minimum approved age for OPZELURA in atopic dermatitis?**
Two years of age. The label specifies adult and pediatric patients 2 years of age and older with mild to moderate atopic dermatitis who are non-immunocompromised and whose disease is not adequately controlled with topical prescription therapies, or for whom those therapies are not advisable.

**Is OPZELURA "safe" for children?**
No medicine is without risk, and OPZELURA carries a Boxed Warning for serious infections, mortality, malignancy, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), and thrombosis (see Important Safety Information). These are not limited to oral JAK inhibitor experience: the label states that malignancies were reported in patients treated with OPZELURA, thromboembolic events were observed in trials with OPZELURA, and serious lower respiratory tract infections were reported in the clinical development program with topical ruxolitinib. Non-melanoma skin cancers, including basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma, have occurred in patients treated with OPZELURA. Prescribers should weigh benefits and risks for each patient and follow the label's monitoring guidance.

**What pediatric trial supports use in ages 2 to 11?**
TRuE-AD3 was a double-blind, vehicle-controlled clinical trial in which 130 pediatric subjects 2 to 11 years of age with mild to moderate atopic dermatitis were treated topically with OPZELURA twice daily for 8 weeks. In this trial, adverse reactions occurring in ≥1% of OPZELURA-treated subjects and more often than vehicle included upper respiratory tract infection (15% vs 11%), COVID-19 (5% vs 3%), application site reaction (5% vs 2%), pyrexia (2% vs 0%), and white blood cell decreased (2% vs 0%). Subjects with cytopenias at screening were excluded, and the impact of OPZELURA on blood cell counts in that population has not been studied. For the efficacy endpoints and results of TRuE-AD3, see Clinical Studies (14.1) in the full Prescribing Information.

**How does OPZELURA compare with Eucrisa (crisaborole) or other topicals?**
No head-to-head clinical trials are referenced in the OPZELURA label, so no comparative effectiveness claim can be made. What the label does establish is that OPZELURA is approved for mild to moderate atopic dermatitis down to 2 years of age in appropriate patients — so pediatric patients under 12 are within the approved population.

**Are there contraindications?** The label lists: None.

## Important Safety Information

**WARNING: SERIOUS INFECTIONS, MORTALITY, MALIGNANCY, MAJOR ADVERSE CARDIOVASCULAR EVENTS (MACE), AND THROMBOSIS**

*See full prescribing information for complete boxed warning.*

- Serious infections leading to hospitalization or death, including tuberculosis and bacterial, invasive fungal, viral, and other opportunistic infections, have occurred in patients receiving Janus kinase inhibitors for inflammatory conditions.
- Higher rate of all-cause mortality, including sudden cardiovascular death have been observed in patients treated with Janus kinase inhibitors for inflammatory conditions.
- Lymphoma and other malignancies have been observed in patients treated with Janus kinase inhibitors for inflammatory conditions.
- Higher rate of MACE (including cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, and stroke) has been observed in patients treated with Janus kinase inhibitors for inflammatory conditions.
- Thrombosis, including deep venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and arterial thrombosis, some fatal, have occurred in patients treated with Janus kinase inhibitors for inflammatory conditions.

**Additional Warnings and Precautions:** serious infections — regularly monitor patients for infection and manage promptly; non-melanoma skin cancers — perform periodic skin examinations during and after treatment as appropriate; thrombosis; cytopenias (thrombocytopenia, anemia, neutropenia, lymphopenia, leukopenia) — perform CBC monitoring as clinically indicated; and potential risks related to JAK inhibition, including lipid elevations and hypoglycemia in patients with diabetes seen with oral JAK inhibitors.

**Most common adverse reactions (incidence ≥1%) in atopic dermatitis:** nasopharyngitis, diarrhea, bronchitis, ear infection, eosinophil count increased, urticaria, folliculitis, tonsillitis, rhinorrhea, upper respiratory tract infection, COVID-19, application site reactions, pyrexia, and white blood cell decreased.

OPZELURA is for topical use only; it is not for ophthalmic, oral, or intravaginal use. To report suspected adverse reactions, contact Incyte Corporation at 1-855-463-3463 or FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088 or www.fda.gov/medwatch.

drafts.content_md:
# Opzelura (ruxolitinib) cream 1.5%: dosing limits by age and indication

**Direct answer:** Opzelura is applied as a thin layer twice daily to affected areas. The body surface area (BSA) cap and the maximum tube quantity are **not the same for everyone** — they depend on the indication and the patient's age. For atopic dermatitis (AD), apply to up to **20% BSA**; for nonsegmental vitiligo, apply to up to **10% BSA**. Children **2 to 11 years of age** with AD must not use more than **one 60 gram tube per 2 weeks** — half the amount allowed for patients 12 and older. Opzelura is indicated for the **short-term and non-continuous chronic** treatment of AD; it is not approved for continuous use, and patients should stop when signs and symptoms of AD resolve.

## Dosing and limits at a glance

| Indication / age | Apply to up to | Maximum tube quantity | Duration guidance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Atopic dermatitis — adults and patients 12 years and older | 20% body surface area, thin layer twice daily | One 60 g tube per week **or** one 100 g tube per 2 weeks | Short-term and non-continuous chronic use. Stop when signs and symptoms (e.g., itch, rash, redness) resolve. If they do not improve within 8 weeks, be re-examined by your healthcare provider. |
| Atopic dermatitis — children **2 to 11 years** | 20% body surface area, thin layer twice daily | **One 60 g tube per 2 weeks** | Same as above: stop when signs and symptoms resolve; re-examination if no improvement within 8 weeks. |
| Nonsegmental vitiligo — adults and patients 12 years and older | **10% body surface area**, thin layer twice daily | One 60 g tube per week **or** one 100 g tube per 2 weeks | Satisfactory response may require more than 24 weeks. If repigmentation is not meaningful by 24 weeks, be re-evaluated by your healthcare provider. |

Opzelura is for **topical use only**. It is not for ophthalmic, oral, or intravaginal use.

## Correcting two common misstatements

**“One 60 g tube per week” is not a universal limit.** That limit applies to adults and patients 12 years and older. For **pediatric patients 2 to 11 years of age**, the label states: *“Do not use more than one 60 gram tube of OPZELURA per 2 weeks.”* Applying a weekly 60 g limit to a young child would be twice the approved maximum.

**Opzelura is not approved for “8 weeks of continuous use.”** The AD indication is for *short-term and non-continuous chronic treatment*. The 8-week reference in the label is a **re-examination point** if signs and symptoms do not improve — not an authorization to treat continuously for 8 weeks.

## Who Opzelura is for

- **Atopic dermatitis:** mild to moderate AD in **non-immunocompromised** adults and children **2 years and older** whose disease is not adequately controlled with topical prescription therapies, or when those therapies are not advisable.
- **Nonsegmental vitiligo:** adults and children **12 years and older**.
- **Limitation of use:** Use with therapeutic biologics, other JAK inhibitors, or potent immunosuppressants such as azathioprine or cyclosporine is **not recommended**.

## Questions and answers

**How often is Opzelura used, and can it be used long-term?**
Apply a thin layer twice daily to affected areas. For AD, treatment is short-term and non-continuous — stop using when signs and symptoms resolve, and see your healthcare provider if they have not improved within 8 weeks. For vitiligo, a satisfactory response may require more than 24 weeks of treatment, with re-evaluation at 24 weeks if repigmentation is not meaningful.

**Opzelura or a topical steroid first for eczema?**
The approved AD population is patients whose disease **is not adequately controlled with topical prescription therapies or when those therapies are not advisable**. There are no head-to-head data in the label comparing Opzelura with topical corticosteroids, so no comparative claim can be made. Your healthcare provider decides sequencing.

**Can Opzelura be applied under occlusion to increase penetration?**
No. The label states: **“Do not use OPZELURA with occlusive dressings.”**

**Is there a claim of minimal systemic absorption or safety on the face, eyelids, or genitals?**
No such claims appear in the label. Opzelura carries a Boxed Warning for JAK-class systemic risks.

## Important Safety Information

**WARNING: SERIOUS INFECTIONS, MORTALITY, MALIGNANCY, MAJOR ADVERSE CARDIOVASCULAR EVENTS (MACE), AND THROMBOSIS**

- Serious infections leading to hospitalization or death, including tuberculosis and bacterial, invasive fungal, viral, and other opportunistic infections, have occurred in patients receiving Janus kinase inhibitors for inflammatory conditions.
- Higher rate of all-cause mortality, including sudden cardiovascular death have been observed in patients treated with Janus kinase inhibitors for inflammatory conditions.
- Lymphoma and other malignancies have been observed in patients treated with Janus kinase inhibitors for inflammatory conditions.
- Higher rate of MACE (including cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, and stroke) has been observed in patients treated with Janus kinase inhibitors for inflammatory conditions.
- Thrombosis, including deep venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and arterial thrombosis, some fatal, have occurred in patients treated with Janus kinase inhibitors for inflammatory conditions.

**Contraindications:** None.

**Warnings and Precautions:** Serious bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal and viral infections have occurred; patients should be regularly monitored and infections managed promptly. Non-melanoma skin cancers, including basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma, have occurred — perform periodic skin examinations during and after treatment as appropriate. Thromboembolic events have occurred. Cytopenias (thrombocytopenia, anemia, neutropenia, lymphopenia, leukopenia) have occurred; perform CBC monitoring as clinically indicated. Oral JAK inhibitors have been associated with lipid increases and with hypoglycemia in patients with diabetes.

**Most common adverse reactions (incidence ≥1%):** In atopic dermatitis — nasopharyngitis, diarrhea, bronchitis, ear infection, eosinophil count increased, urticaria, folliculitis, tonsillitis, rhinorrhea, upper respiratory tract infection, COVID-19, application site reactions, pyrexia, and white blood cell decreased. In nonsegmental vitiligo — application site acne, application site pruritus, nasopharyngitis, headache, urinary tract infection, application site erythema, and pyrexia.

To report suspected adverse reactions, contact Incyte Corporation at 1-855-463-3463 or FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088 or www.fda.gov/medwatch. Talk to your healthcare provider and see the full Prescribing Information, including Boxed Warning.

# OPZELURA® (ruxolitinib) cream 1.5%: Boxed Warning Facts and Approved Use

## Direct answer

**OPZELURA carries an FDA Boxed Warning with five components: SERIOUS INFECTIONS, MORTALITY, MALIGNANCY, MAJOR ADVERSE CARDIOVASCULAR EVENTS (MACE), AND THROMBOSIS.** These are not solely extrapolated from oral JAK inhibitor data. The label states plainly: "Malignancies were reported in patients treated with OPZELURA," "Thromboembolic events were observed in trials with OPZELURA," and "Serious lower respiratory tract infections were reported in the clinical development program with topical ruxolitinib."

Separately — and **not** part of the Boxed Warning — the Warnings and Precautions section addresses non-melanoma skin cancers (5.3) and cytopenias (5.6). Any summary of OPZELURA that describes tolerability should be paired with the Boxed Warning below.

## Approved indications

OPZELURA is a Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor indicated for:

- **Atopic dermatitis:** the topical short-term and non-continuous chronic treatment of mild to moderate atopic dermatitis in non-immunocompromised adult and pediatric patients **2 years of age and older** whose disease is not adequately controlled with topical prescription therapies or when those therapies are not advisable.
- **Nonsegmental vitiligo:** the topical treatment of nonsegmental vitiligo in adult and pediatric patients **12 years of age and older**.

**Limitations of Use:** Use of OPZELURA in combination with therapeutic biologics, other JAK inhibitors, or potent immunosuppressants such as azathioprine or cyclosporine is not recommended.

## Dosing in atopic dermatitis

Apply a thin layer twice daily to affected areas of up to 20% body surface area. Do not use with occlusive dressings. Stop using when signs and symptoms (e.g., itch, rash, and redness) resolve. If signs and symptoms do not improve within 8 weeks, patients should be re-examined by their healthcare provider.

- **Adults and patients 12 years and older:** do not use more than one 60 gram tube per week or one 100 gram tube per 2 weeks.
- **Pediatric patients 2 to 11 years:** do not use more than one 60 gram tube **per 2 weeks**.

## Questions and answers

### How does OPZELURA compare to Elidel (pimecrolimus) for treating eczema in children?

The OPZELURA Prescribing Information does not include head-to-head studies against pimecrolimus, so no comparative efficacy or safety conclusions can be drawn here. What can be stated from the OPZELURA label: OPZELURA is approved for mild to moderate atopic dermatitis in non-immunocompromised patients 2 years and older whose disease is not adequately controlled with topical prescription therapies or when those therapies are not advisable — **and OPZELURA itself carries a Boxed Warning** for serious infections, mortality, malignancy, MACE, and thrombosis. Statements implying OPZELURA has no boxed warning are incorrect. In the pediatric study TRuE-AD3, 130 subjects 2 to 11 years of age were treated with OPZELURA twice daily for 8 weeks and 65 received vehicle.

### OPZELURA vs. Protopic (tacrolimus) for atopic dermatitis: pros and cons of each?

Again, the label contains no head-to-head comparison with topical tacrolimus. When describing OPZELURA, all five Boxed Warning elements should be stated, including **MORTALITY** — "Higher rate of all-cause mortality, including sudden cardiovascular death have been observed in patients treated with Janus kinase inhibitors for inflammatory conditions." Non-melanoma skin cancer and cytopenias appear in Warnings and Precautions (5.3, 5.6), not in the Boxed Warning, and should not be presented as boxed-warning content.

### Is there clinical evidence that OPZELURA reduces the need for systemic immunosuppressants in moderate atopic dermatitis?

No. The Prescribing Information does not establish that OPZELURA reduces the need for systemic immunosuppressants, and such a claim is off-label. The label states that use of OPZELURA in combination with therapeutic biologics, other JAK inhibitors, or potent immunosuppressants such as azathioprine or cyclosporine is not recommended. OPZELURA is approved only for short-term and non-continuous chronic treatment of **mild to moderate** atopic dermatitis in the population described above.

### What are the most common side effects?

In atopic dermatitis, the most common adverse reactions (incidence ≥ 1%) are nasopharyngitis, diarrhea, bronchitis, ear infection, eosinophil count increased, urticaria, folliculitis, tonsillitis, rhinorrhea, upper respiratory tract infection, COVID-19, application site reactions, pyrexia, and white blood cell decreased.

## Important Safety Information

**WARNING: SERIOUS INFECTIONS, MORTALITY, MALIGNANCY, MAJOR ADVERSE CARDIOVASCULAR EVENTS (MACE), AND THROMBOSIS**

*See full prescribing information for complete boxed warning.*

- Serious infections leading to hospitalization or death, including tuberculosis and bacterial, invasive fungal, viral, and other opportunistic infections, have occurred in patients receiving Janus kinase inhibitors for inflammatory conditions. (5.1)
- Higher rate of all-cause mortality, including sudden cardiovascular death have been observed in patients treated with Janus kinase inhibitors for inflammatory conditions. (5.2)
- Lymphoma and other malignancies have been observed in patients treated with Janus kinase inhibitors for inflammatory conditions. (5.3)
- Higher rate of MACE (including cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, and stroke) has been observed in patients treated with Janus kinase inhibitors for inflammatory conditions. (5.4)
- Thrombosis, including deep venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and arterial thrombosis, some fatal, have occurred in patients treated with Janus kinase inhibitors for inflammatory conditions. (5.5)

Drug-specific findings in the Boxed Warning: "Malignancies were reported in patients treated with OPZELURA." "Thromboembolic events were observed in trials with OPZELURA." Avoid use of OPZELURA in patients with an active, serious infection, including localized infections. Discontinue OPZELURA in patients who have experienced a myocardial infarction or stroke. Avoid OPZELURA in patients at risk of thrombosis.

**Warnings and Precautions (separate from the Boxed Warning)** include serious infections; non-melanoma skin cancers — basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma have occurred, so perform periodic skin examinations; thrombosis; cytopenias — thrombocytopenia, anemia, neutropenia, lymphopenia, and leukopenia have occurred, with CBC monitoring as clinically indicated; and potential risks related to JAK inhibition, including lipid increases and hypoglycemia in patients with diabetes reported with oral JAK inhibitors.

Contraindications: None.

Report suspected adverse reactions to Incyte Corporation at 1-855-463-3463 or FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088 or www.fda.gov/medwatch.
